name: P.14

origin.place: Research Institute of Pomology (now Research Institute of Horticulture), Skierniewice
origin.parentage: reported as an open-pollinated seedling of M.9
origin.note: Product of the Skierniewice programme that crossed M.9, M.4 and M.11 with hardy Antonovka and Longfield.

support: Stake young trees; spindle trees usually kept on a wire
soil_notes: recommended in Poland for lighter, poorer soils; on rich alluvial soil trees can grow larger than on M.7
best_for: semi-dwarf orchard trees on light soils; replacement for M.26, M.7 and MM.106 in Poland
avoid_when: very fertile soils where trees become too large for intensive spacing
variety_fit: Strong growth suits weak or spur-type varieties; vigorous varieties may grow too big on good land.
notes: Polish semi-dwarf slightly more vigorous than M.26 on light soil, but more than twice the size of M.9 trees (larger than M.7) on rich soil near Warsaw. Trees start cropping in year two and give high per-tree yields, though yield efficiency is low; it roots better in stoolbeds than M.26 and is one of the most planted semi-dwarfs in Poland. Moderately winter-hardy with medium mildew and fire blight susceptibility.

name: P.16

origin.place: Research Institute of Pomology (now Research Institute of Horticulture), Skierniewice

support: Permanent stake or trellis; wood is brittle
soil_notes: needs fertile, well-managed, irrigated soil; too weak for light or grassed ground
best_for: very high-density plantings on good soil; small garden trees
avoid_when: poor or dry soils, cold-winter sites, fire-blight areas
variety_fit: Pairs with vigorous scions; fruit was smaller than on M.9 with some varieties.
notes: Dwarfing Polish stock between M.27 and M.9 in vigour (trunk area roughly a third to two-thirds that of M.9) with the highest cropping efficiency in several Polish trials but low yield per tree. Produced no suckers or burr knots in an 11-year Skierniewice trial and was recommended there alongside M.9 T337 for Golden Delicious Reinders. Early Geneva work found it brittle, and Polish pomologists regarded it as less winter-hardy than other P stocks.

name: P.22

origin.place: Research Institute of Pomology (now Research Institute of Horticulture), Skierniewice

soil_notes: needs fertile, weed-free, irrigated soil like M.27
best_for: very small trees, containers and super-dense plantings in cold regions; hardy dwarfing interstem
avoid_when: poor, dry or grassed ground; woolly aphid or fire-blight hot spots; weak scion varieties
variety_fit: Only vigorous varieties make a worthwhile tree; fruit tended to be smaller than on M.9.
notes: Polish super-dwarf in the M.27 size class, very precocious, with few suckers or burr knots and good crown-rot resistance. In a 1971/72 Polish freeze fewer than a quarter of P 22 plants were damaged against over 85% of M.9. Yields per tree are low and fruit tends to be small; it is very susceptible to woolly aphid and moderately to highly susceptible to fire blight.

name: Supporter 4

origin.note: Clonal selection of the older Pillnitz clone Pi 80 from W. Schindler's 1930s Paradise x Doucin crosses (Cummins and Aldwinckle 1982 suggested M.9 x M.2); named Supporter 4 in M. Fischer's Pillnitz programme.

support: Stake or single wire; anchorage better than M.9, similar to M.26
soil_notes: general orchard soils; a stronger root than M.9 for sites where M.9 is too weak
best_for: intensive and semi-intensive orchards in M.26 size class; replacing M.26 where M.9 is unsuitable
avoid_when: fire-blight areas; super-high-density systems needing M.9-sized trees
notes: German semi-dwarf from Dresden-Pillnitz with vigour close to M.26, varying with cultivar. It crops early, is more yield-efficient than M.26 and MM.106 though less than M.9, makes fewer burr knots than M.26 and roots more easily in stoolbeds than M.9 or M.26. Good winter-frost resistance in European reports; NC-140 trials found survival and size similar to M.26 after five years; fire blight susceptible.

name: Alnarp 2

origin.place: Alnarp Fruit Tree Station (now SLU Alnarp), Skane, southern Sweden
origin.parentage: selected from a group of mixed Doucin (paradise-type) trees
origin.note: Selected in 1920, released in 1944 and brought to North America in 1949.

soil_notes: prone to magnesium deficiency; avoid wet, Phytophthora-prone ground
best_for: large free-standing trees and hardy interstem frames in northern climates
avoid_when: small gardens; wet soils; fire-blight regions
notes: Old Swedish clonal stock of Doucin type, widely used in Scandinavia and the Baltics for its winter hardiness and easy stoolbed propagation. It makes large free-standing trees about 85-90% of seedling size (roughly MM.111 class) and Canadian reports describe it as fairly precocious for its vigour. Susceptible to fire blight, collar rot and woolly aphid, and sensitive to magnesium deficiency.

name: Ottawa 3

origin.place: Agriculture Canada Research Station (Central Experimental Farm), Ottawa, Ontario
origin.note: Described by Spangelo, Fejer and Granger in 1974; later used as a parent of G.935.

support: Stake or trellis; better anchored and much less brittle than M.9
soil_notes: fertile, well-drained soil; collar-rot resistance similar to M.9
best_for: dwarf trees in cold-winter regions; hardy dwarfing interstem
avoid_when: fire-blight areas; scions carrying apple stem grooving virus
variety_fit: Use certified virus-free scionwood, as the stock is sensitive to apple stem grooving virus.
notes: Canadian hardy dwarf between M.9 and M.26 in size, precocious and productive, with yield efficiency usually above M.26 but below M.9; fruit was occasionally a little smaller. In cold-hardiness tests it tolerated about -35 C but not -40 C. It roots poorly in stoolbeds (often micropropagated), rarely suckers, resists collar rot but is susceptible to fire blight and woolly aphid.

name: Mark

origin.place: Michigan State University, East Lansing, Michigan
origin.note: Selected and tested as MAC-9 by Robert F. Carlson; introduced 1979-80 and covered by US Plant Patent 4678.

support: Support recommended; early claims of free-standing trees did not hold on many sites
soil_notes: very drought-sensitive: irrigate even where irrigation is normally optional
best_for: historical interest; existing plantings on irrigated, fertile sites
avoid_when: hot, dry or unirrigated sites; new plantings (better dwarfing stocks exist)
notes: Michigan dwarf from an M.9 seedling, very precocious and often more yield-efficient than M.9 T337 in its early years. Older trees commonly develop root mass proliferation, a tumour-like swelling at or below the soil line that stunts them and makes performance highly variable; it is also very drought-sensitive and did poorly in hot, dry western regions. Hardy in early winter but prone to late-winter injury, fire blight and woolly aphid susceptible, fairly crown-rot resistant, and has largely fallen out of commercial use.
